blocks.text: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation: The Math That Decides the Design
The two-minute estimation skill behind every good design: state your assumptions, round shamelessly, multiply, and sanity-check — the method Fermi used to weigh an atomic blast with falling paper.
A bomb, some confetti, and sixty seconds

July 16, 1945, New Mexico desert, just before dawn. Enrico Fermi — one of the great physicists of the century — is standing at base camp, about ten miles from a tower holding the first atomic bomb ever built. In his hand: a few scraps of torn-up paper.

The bomb goes off. Flash, heat, the pillar of smoke climbing past the clouds. About forty seconds later, the blast wave arrives — and Fermi does something that looks like a magic trick. He drops his paper scraps from about six feet up, some before the wave arrives, some during, some after, and watches how far the falling pieces get pushed sideways. The shift: about two and a half meters. From that — paper, falling, in a desert — he announces his estimate: the blast was equivalent to ten thousand tons of TNT.

He was right where it mattered. The instruments that survived the test put the blast energy at roughly his figure, and the total yield, once the soil samples were analyzed, came to about 18,600 tons — the same order of magnitude, from a man dropping confetti. Fermi wrote the whole observation up in a short memorandum that survives in the U.S. National Archives.

This lesson is about that skill. Not the physics — the estimation: getting a useful number, fast, from almost nothing, and knowing how much to trust it. Fermi didn't have a gift. He had a method, and the method is learnable. By the end of this lesson you'll have it.
Why this matters

In the framework lesson, Step 2 — sketch the route — asks for "the back-of-envelope math": two minutes of arithmetic against the scope from Step 1 that tells you which boxes need to be distributed and which are fine as a single instance. This lesson is that math, taught properly.

Here's why it decides designs. Every architecture question is secretly a size question in disguise. "Do we need a cache?" depends on how many reads per second are coming. "Can one database hold this?" depends on how many bytes a year you're adding. "Is fan-out going to kill us?" depends on one multiplication. Candidates who estimate look like engineers; candidates who skip it are drawing pictures. Interviewers know the difference, which is why the framework lesson lists "skipping the math" as a Step 2 anti-pattern with its own name.

The good news: estimation math is not real math. There are no integrals. There is rounding, multiplying round numbers, and checking that the answer isn't absurd. If you can estimate what a suitcase weighs before the airline scale proves you wrong, you already have the core skill — this lesson just gives you reference weights and a routine.
The suitcase scale
This lesson's running analogy: estimating is weighing a suitcase by hand.

You've done it at an airport. You lift the case, compare it against weights you know — a bag of sugar is a kilo, a big dog is thirty — and you say "that's about eighteen kilos." You're never exact. You don't need to be. You need to know whether it's 5, 18, or 45, because each of those means a different decision: carry-on, check it, or pay the fee and rethink your life choices.
System estimation works identically:

Reference weights are the handful of numbers you memorize — how long a memory read takes, how many seconds are in a day, what a kilobyte of text looks like. (The next lesson, the companion reference, is the full set. This lesson teaches you to lift.)

Rounding is packing light. Nobody weighs a suitcase to the gram before a flight, and nobody estimates with 4.7 × 10⁸ users. You say "about 500 million" and move on — the rounding is not sloppiness, it's the technique.
The sanity check is the second lift. "Eighteen kilos" — plausible. "A hundred and eighty" — you put the case down and think again. Every estimate in this lesson ends with that second lift.
The method: four moves
Every back-of-envelope calculation, from Fermi's paper to a Google interview room, is the same four moves in order.

Move 1 — Say the assumptions out loud. Users, reads versus writes, bytes per item, how long you keep things. Assumptions are the estimate; the arithmetic is clerical. Stating them out loud does two things: it lets the interviewer correct a wrong one before it poisons everything downstream ("actually, assume a million users, not a hundred million"), and it converts your guesses into shared decisions — exactly the Step 1 habit from the framework lesson.

Move 2 — Round to friendly numbers. Powers of ten and near-powers: 100 million users, 2 posts each, 1 KB per post. Keep one significant digit if you must, zero if you can. Friendly numbers multiply in your head without a calculator, and the interviewer can follow every step — an estimate nobody can follow earns no credit, however accurate it secretly is.

Move 3 — Multiply through, carrying the units. Users × posts per user = posts. Posts ÷ seconds = posts per second. Posts × bytes = storage. The units are your guardrails: if you end up holding "users per byte," you divided somewhere you should have multiplied. One gift to memorize now: a day is about 100,000 seconds (86,400, rounded the Fermi way). Almost every "per day" figure becomes "per second" with a single division by 10⁵, and per-second is the unit designs are built in.

Move 4 — Sanity-check the order of magnitude. Ask: is this answer the right size of answer? A consumer app doing 10,000 writes a second is plausible; 10 billion is a supercomputer wearing a trench coat. Compare against anchors you trust — the framework lesson sized a URL shortener at about 40 writes a second from 100M URLs a month. If your estimate for a similar system lands a thousand times away from a known anchor, the bug is in your assumptions, not in the world.

Notice the loop. A failed sanity check doesn't mean start over — it means one assumption was off, and finding it is the most impressive thing you can do in the room. Fermi's speed looks like Move 4 performed in advance: historians reconstruct that he had already worked out what a given paper displacement would mean before the test (that reconstruction is Katz's, in Sources — Fermi's own memo records only the observation and the answer). Either way, the estimate was fast because the thinking was already done. That's the job of the next section: do the thinking now, so the interview version takes two minutes.
Reference weights: the latency ladder in human time

One set of reference weights matters more than any other: how long the machine itself takes to do things. These are the famous latency numbers — published by Peter Norvig, taught at Google from Jeff Dean's talks — and they span such absurd ranges (a memory read is a hundred thousand times faster than a disk seek) that raw nanoseconds stop meaning anything. So let's weigh the headline rungs on the suitcase scale: if fetching from the fastest cache took one second, here's how long the rest takes. (The full table — every rung, with the sources — is the companion reference lesson that follows this one.)
Operation, Real time, If an L1 cache fetch = 1 second
L1 cache reference, 0.5 ns, 1 second
Main memory reference, 100 ns, about 3 minutes
Read from a modern SSD (random), about 50 µs, about a day
Round trip inside one datacenter, about 0.5 ms, about 12 days
Disk seek (spinning disk), about 10 ms, about 8 months
Packet: California → Netherlands → back, about 150 ms, about 9½ years

Read the ladder the way an engineer reads it. Anything measured in minutes is basically free — that's why we cache in memory and never apologize for it. Anything measured in days is a design decision: an SSD read per request might be fine, a million of them is a queue. Anything measured in months or years must never happen on the user's path at all — a single disk seek or cross-ocean round trip, multiplied by real traffic, is how systems fall over. Every caching layer, every CDN, every "keep it in one region" decision you'll meet in this course is somebody respecting this ladder.

Two honest footnotes. First, the SSD rung has moved since the classic table was written: Dean-era SSDs took about 150 µs (three and a half days, human-scale); modern NVMe drives do it in the tens of microseconds — same rung of the ladder, better shoes. The gaps between rungs have barely moved in fifteen years, and the gaps are the lesson. Second, one rung can never improve: the transatlantic packet is bounded by the speed of light. Nine and a half years is physics, not engineering debt.

The person who taught the world to feel these numbers was Rear Admiral Grace Hopper, who carried pieces of wire cut to the distance light travels in a nanosecond — 11.8 inches — and handed them out in lectures so programmers would know what they were throwing away when they threw away microseconds. War story: the website that met America unprepared
Now the Fermi story told backwards — what happens when nobody does the envelope math.

October 1, 2013: HealthCare.gov launches. It's the front door for a country's health insurance marketplace — about as high-stakes as a launch gets, with a date fixed by law and a president's signature policy riding on it. Millions of people showed up on day one. The site collapsed almost immediately: error pages, frozen accounts, queues that went nowhere. By the end of the first day, the number of people who had actually managed to enroll was six.

The postmortems — and there were many, including a full Government Accountability Office review — did not find one villainous bug. They found something more instructive: the estimation and testing loop this lesson teaches was never closed. GAO's report is blunt: end-to-end testing of the whole system did not occur before launch, and pieces were still being finished as the date arrived. And the load testing that did happen was sized by hope rather than arithmetic: the identity system that every single visitor had to pass through — the site's front door — had been load-tested at roughly 2,000 simultaneous users, while the demand the launch actually faced was in the tens of thousands at once, on its way to millions of visits that first day.

Run the envelope math they skipped. It's three lines, all from this lesson. The administration later reported about 4.7 million visitors on day one. Spread over even a generous 10-hour peak, that's about 150 arrivals a second. Now the move nobody made: each visitor stays for minutes — say a 5-minute session — so the number inside at once is 150 × 300 seconds ≈ 45,000 simultaneous users. Tested capacity: 2,000. So even this deliberately gentle envelope says the front door was load-tested at roughly one twenty-fifth of the crowd it should have expected. And the envelope was the optimistic version: the documented record is worse. The administration's technology chief later put the actual peak at roughly 250,000 people on the site at once — more than a hundred times the tested load. Fermi with paper scraps got within a factor of two of an atomic bomb. A program with hundreds of engineers and a nine-figure budget under-tested its front door by a factor of twenty-five on the kindest arithmetic, because the estimate either never happened or never traveled.

The rescue is the postscript that proves the rule: the "tech surge" team that fixed the site in the following weeks worked by instrumenting everything, measuring real numbers daily, and burning down a list ordered by measured impact. They didn't write heroic code first. They estimated, measured, and only then engineered. That's the order this lesson teaches — and it's the order Step 2 of the framework assumes.
Worked example: sizing a Twitter-shaped service

Enough stories. Let's run the four moves on the kind of prompt interviews actually give — "design a social posting service" — and watch an estimate steer real design decisions. Every number is an assumption, stated out loud, per Move 1.

The assumptions. 100 million daily active users. Each posts twice a day on average. A post, stored with its metadata, is about 1 KB. Each user reads a hundred posts a day — timelines, replies, profiles. Peak traffic runs about 5× the average. None of these are facts about any real company; they're the scope we'd agree with the interviewer in Step 1, and changing them changes the design, which is the point.

Writes. 100M users × 2 posts = 200M posts a day. Divide by our gift number, 100,000 seconds in a day: about 2,000 posts a second on average, about 10,000 a second at peak. Verdict from the ladder of experience: a write rate a small fleet handles without heroics. Writes are not the problem.

Storage. 200M posts × 1 KB = 200 GB of new posts a day. × 365 ≈ 73 TB a year — round it to about 100 TB a year once indexes and a couple of replicas join in. Verdict: real storage, but ordinary. A few dozen drives a year. Storage is not the problem either.

Reads. 100M users × 100 posts read = 10 billion reads a day. ÷ 100,000 seconds = 100,000 reads a second, half a million at peak — fifty reads for every write. There is the design. A read rate like that decides the architecture before any box is drawn: timelines must be served from memory or cache, not computed from the database per request, and the fan-out question — when someone with ten million followers posts, do we push that post into ten million timelines now, or pull it into each reader's timeline at read time? — is exactly the deep-dive target Step 3 exists for. Notice the estimate didn't just produce numbers. It located the hard part, which is what Step 2's math is for.

Sanity check (Move 4). Does 100,000 reads a second hold up against anchors? The framework lesson's URL shortener — 100M URLs a month — came out at about 400 reads a second, and it was a deliberately modest service. A global social network at 250× that read rate, with fifty-to-one read skew, matches the shape of every real system in this genre you've read about. The estimate is the right size of answer — which is all an estimate ever promises: the order of magnitude is where it needs to land, and it lands there.
Practice, in interview form
Three prompts. For each, the deliverable is what an interviewer wants: the one-line estimate, with its assumptions said out loud. Cover the answers and try first.

"How much storage does a URL shortener need in its first year?" Assume 100M new URLs a month (from the framework lesson) at about 500 bytes a record. → 100M × 12 = 1.2 billion records × 500 B ≈ 600 GB a year — a single modest database, no sharding heroics on day one.

"How many messages a second must a chat service carry?" Assume 50M daily users sending 40 messages each. → 2 billion messages a day ÷ 100,000 ≈ 20,000 messages a second average; design for about 100,000 at peak.

"What network bandwidth does a photo service need just for uploads?" Assume 1M uploads a day at 2 MB each. → 2 TB a day ÷ 100,000 seconds = 20 MB a second ≈ 160 Mbps of pure upload traffic, before anyone downloads a single photo.

If your answers came out within a factor of two or three of these, you did it right — that's the tolerance this skill runs at. If one came out a hundred times off, find which assumption moved; that's Move 4 earning its keep.
Dos and don'ts
Do:
Say every assumption out loud. The assumptions are the estimate. Silent numbers look like guesses; stated assumptions look like engineering.
Round early and openly. "Call it a hundred million users" is a sentence interviewers love — it shows you know which digits don't matter.
Carry the units. Posts per day ÷ seconds per day = posts per second. Units catch the multiply-versus-divide slips that sink estimates.
End with the sanity check. Anchor against a system you already sized. Landing near a trusted anchor is your proof of work.
Let the estimate steer. The numbers exist to make decisions — "so reads dominate fifty to one, which means the budget goes to caching." Say that sentence.
Don't:
Don't reach for a calculator voice. Precise-looking numbers (4,173 posts/sec) signal false precision. Round numbers signal judgment.
Don't estimate in private. Two silent minutes of arithmetic is the silent-cartographer anti-pattern wearing a math costume. Narrate every move.
Don't skip the peak. Averages design demos; peaks design systems. State your peak multiplier as an assumption and use it.
Don't defend a broken anchor. If the interviewer corrects an assumption ("make it a billion users"), redo the one multiplication live and move on. Adjusting fast is the skill being graded.
Don't estimate what you won't use. If no decision depends on a number, don't compute it. Estimation is a steering wheel, not a decoration.
Takeaways

Estimation is a method, not a talent: state assumptions, round to friendly numbers, multiply through with units, sanity-check the order of magnitude. Fermi weighed a bomb blast with falling paper using exactly these moves.
A day holds about 100,000 seconds. That one rounding converts almost any "per day" figure into the per-second units designs are built in.
The latency ladder in human time: memory ≈ minutes, an SSD read ≈ a day, a disk seek ≈ months, an ocean crossing ≈ years. Designs are mostly the art of keeping the slow rungs off the user's path.

HealthCare.gov is the cautionary tale: a front door tested at about 2,000 simultaneous users met tens of thousands, because the three-line estimate either never happened or never traveled. The rescue team fixed it by measuring first.
A good estimate locates the hard part. In the worked example, writes and storage were ordinary — the 50-to-1 read skew was the design. Finding that in minute ten is the whole game.

The full reference weights — the complete latency table, the powers-of-two ladder, and the availability "nines" with their downtime math — live in the companion lesson that follows this one, Estimation Reference Numbers, built to be linked from every case study in this course.
